verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, upon Shoshannim, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung to the tune called Lilies: a song of David's.
verses.directors_commentary:
This line is a stage direction, not part of the speech, and the actors should know that the cry that follows has a performance setting. The Hebrew counts it as verse 1, which is why every verse in this psalm is numbered one higher than in the KJV, which prints it as an unnumbered heading and starts at 69:1 with 'Save me'.

Nobody is sure what 'Shoshannim' (lilies) was. Ibn Ezra takes it as the opening words of a poem, a known tune the psalm was to be sung to. Meiri and Metzudat Zion take it as a musical instrument, Metzudat Zion adding that it was shaped like a lily. Rashi reads it as a message: Israel is the lily among thorns of Song 2:2, and the thorns prick it, so the psalm prays for them. The KJV's 'upon Shoshannim' just leaves the word untranslated. Do not play the word as a mood; it is a label. The lily reading is available for a director who wants it, and should be chosen openly.

philological_notes.note: 'Lilies', in the plural, also in the headings of Psalms 45 and 80. Read as a tune: Ibn Ezra takes it as the opening of a poem the psalm was sung to. Read as an instrument: Meiri and Metzudat Zion, who describes it as lily-shaped. Read as a symbol: Rashi, Israel among thorns. The Hebrew does not decide between them.

'To the choirmaster', a participle of the root that means to excel, or to be pre-eminent. It appears in the headings of fifty-five psalms, and marks the psalm as handed over to the one who directs the Temple music.

verses.translation_literal: Save me, God, for waters have come up to the throat.
verses.translation_dramatic: Save me, O God. The water has risen. It is at my throat.
verses.directors_commentary: The first word is a command in the imperative, with no greeting and no praise: 'Save me.' Play it as a shout from someone standing in a flood. Water is the Hebrew Bible's ordinary picture of chaos and death, so a listener hears more than a river. Hebrew 'nefesh' means 'soul' in the KJV's 'unto my soul', but its first sense is the breathing throat, and BBE's 'to my neck' is nearer the picture: the water has reached the place where the breath goes in. Radak and Metzudat David both read it so, as water at the neck of a man about to drown. The KJV's 'are come in' also adds a direction the Hebrew lacks; the waters 'have come', and the verb needs no 'in'. 'Elohim' is the plain word for God, not yet the covenant name, which waits until verse 7.

philological_notes.note: Throat, breath, life, self. With 'to' and water it means the throat: the water has reached the neck and the breathing place, which is how Radak on Psalm 69:2 and Metzudat David on Psalm 69:2 take it.

verses.translation_literal: I have sunk in the mire of the depth, and there is no foothold; I have come into the depths of water, and a flood has overflowed me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have gone down into mud that has no bottom, and there is nothing under my feet to stand on. I have walked into the deep water, and the flood has closed over me.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker tells the danger in three steps, as Malbim counts them: mud that holds the feet, water too deep to stand in, and a current that carries the body off. Stage it as three blows, not one picture. 'Yaven' is soft clay, the muck at a riverbed (Metzudat Zion calls it the filth on the bottom), and the speaker is stuck in it before he is swimming. 'Mo'amad' ('foothold') comes from the verb 'to stand'; Radak even takes it as 'no part of my body that can stand', and the point is that nothing in his own body can hold him up, let alone the ground. The KJV's 'deep waters' for 'ma'amakkei mayim' is fair, but 'where the floods overflow me' turns a plain flood into a place. 'Shibbolet' here is a rushing stream; it is the same word that is an ear of grain elsewhere, and a flood in Isa 27:12 (cited by Metzudat Zion). Radak and Metzudat David both note that a man can drown in a river that is shallow if it runs fast, and in deep water that is still: this speaker has both.

philological_notes.note: Here a flood or rushing current, not an ear of grain; Metzudat Zion compares Isa 27:12 and Rashi glosses it as the strong stream of a river.
Soft mud at the bottom of water, the sucking clay in which a person sinks; Metzudat Zion defines it as the filth at the bottom of the water.
A standing place, a foothold; a noun from the verb 'to stand'. Radak takes it as a causative noun, 'something that makes one stand'.

verses.translation_literal: I am weary in my calling; my throat is parched; my eyes have failed, waiting for my God.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have cried until there is nothing left in me to cry with. My throat is dry as a riverbed in August, and my eyes, which have watched the sky so long for an answer, have given out. Still I wait for my God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The man in the flood has now been calling for help for so long that his body has begun to fail: first the voice, then the sight. Ancient readers had the picture in front of them. A drowning man shouts to the bank and then looks up, hoping someone will come. Radak and Meiri both read the verse this way, and take the long wait as a figure for the length of the exile. Play the exhaustion, not the panic: the energy of verse 2 has gone.

The KJV's 'my throat is dried' is accurate, and 'mine eyes fail while I wait' is fair, but the KJV softens one thing. Hebrew 'my eyes have failed' (kalu, 'are finished, spent') is the standard idiom for hoping until the hope itself gives out. Rashi quotes Deuteronomy 28:32 and Leviticus 26:16, 'the failing of the eyes', as the same language. It is not 'weak sight' but spent hope. The participle 'waiting' (meyachel) closes the line on the same word it will not give up.

philological_notes.note: 'Parched, burnt dry', a Niphal of the root for heat and dryness. Rashi on Psalm 69:4 glosses it simply 'dry', comparing Job 30:30, and Metzudat Zion on Psalm 69:4 says it means dryness, as in 'the parched places' (chararim) of Jeremiah 17:6. The sense is a throat scorched dry from shouting.

Literally 'my eyes have come to an end'. Rashi on Psalm 69:4 explains that prolonged hope is called the 'finishing of the eyes' and cites Deuteronomy 28:32 and Job 11:20. Metzudat David on Psalm 69:4 says the same of one who waits for something that does not come.

verses.translation_literal: More than the hairs of my head are those who hate me without cause; they are mighty, those who would destroy me, my enemies falsely: that which I did not steal, then I must return.
verses.translation_dramatic: Count the hairs on my head and you will still have counted too few. They hate me for nothing, and they are strong, those who wish me cut off, my enemies by a lie. I am made to hand back what I never took.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker is under attack from two sides at once, by numbers and by law. The hair image is plain hyperbole; the more specific line is the last, where a man is made to pay for goods he never stole. In the ancient Near East a false claim of theft or debt was enough to ruin someone with no protector, and a poor man might pay rather than fight. Metzudat David reads it as restitution forced on him whenever they bring a charge. Radak and Meiri say the same: they accuse him of taking, and impose penalties as if he had. Rashi has a sharper version: when the enemies gather against him he buys them off with money, giving them what he never took from them.

The KJV 'then I restored that which I took not away' turns the clause into a past event and reads like a confession of generosity. The Hebrew is imperfect ('I must return') and has no past tense at all. The KJV also makes 'wrongfully' do double duty for sheker, which means 'falsehood': these are enemies by a lie, not merely unjust ones.

philological_notes.note: 'For nothing, without cause', from the root for favour, so literally 'free of charge'. Metzudat David on Psalm 69:5 explains it as hatred of those to whom he never did harm. Here it names hatred with no reason behind it.

Hiphil participle, 'those who cut me off, silence me, destroy me'. Metzudat Zion on Psalm 69:5 ties it to cutting off, quoting 'every morning I will destroy (atzmit)' from Psalm 101, so these enemies are seeking to end him, not just to harass him.

'Then I must return.' Rashi on Psalm 69:5 reads it as bribery, giving them money when they gather against him. Metzudat David on Psalm 69:5 reads it as forced restitution when they bring false charges. 'Then' (az) is the hard word: it may mean 'at that point, when they accuse', not an earlier time.

verses.translation_literal: God, you, you know my folly, and my guilts from you are not hidden.
verses.translation_dramatic: O God, you know me. You know my folly. And the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you.
verses.directors_commentary: After a verse of claiming innocence before men, the voice turns and confesses before God. The two verses sit side by side and the psalm does not smooth them. The speaker is innocent of the charges, as verse 5 says, but he does not claim to be spotless. Ibn Ezra reads 'you know' as an appeal to the true judge; Metzudat David hears it as a plea that his faults, such as they are, do not merit this much punishment. Play it quiet. The Hebrew puts the pronoun in for emphasis: 'God, you, you know', and the repeated word is the only emphasis the line needs. 'Ivvalti' ('my folly') is a rare noun from the word for the fool; the KJV's 'foolishness' is faithful. 'Ashmotai' is plural, 'my guilts', and the KJV's 'sins' flattens guilt into an act: the Hebrew word names the state of being guilty, the debt that remains. 'Not hidden' closes the verse with the point that nothing is concealed from the One who knows.

philological_notes.note: Folly, the conduct of the fool ('evil'). Radak takes it as foolish speech or conduct; Malbim as doubts that weaken faith; Metzudat Zion as sin done under a spirit of foolishness.
Plural of 'guilt, guilt-offering, liability': the condition of being at fault, not only the deed. Radak reads it as faults of error.

verses.translation_literal: May they not be ashamed in me, those who wait for you, Lord YHWH of hosts; may they not be humiliated in me, those who seek you, God of Israel.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not let those who wait for you be put to shame because of me, Lord, LORD of hosts. Do not let those who seek you be brought low through me, God of Israel.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a bold turn. The speaker no longer asks to be saved for his own sake; he argues that if God lets him sink, everyone who hopes in God will see it and be ashamed. Rashi hears the crowd's mocking voice: 'Is this what happens to one who hoped in the Holy One?' Radak says the same: if my hope fails, the hope of all who hope fails. So this is a plea made on God's reputation. The two halves say the same thing in two words, as Radak says, though Malbim finds a difference: 'shame' is felt in oneself, 'humiliation' is dealt out by others. The God of Israel is named with the whole string of titles, and the stage should grow louder for it: 'Lord YHWH of hosts, God of Israel'. Ibn Ezra reads 'hosts' as the heavenly armies and 'Israel' as His army on earth. The KJV's 'for my sake' is a paraphrase of a little preposition 'in me': the shame is in the speaker, as though his fall were the container of their disgrace.

philological_notes.note: 'Those who wait for you, hope in you': the root also means a cord pulled taut, hope as tension. Metzudat David reads it as those who hope for God.
'Be humiliated'. Malbim separates 'bosh' (shame felt within) from 'klimah' (disgrace before others).
'Hosts, armies'. Ibn Ezra reads them as the heavenly hosts, and 'God of Israel' as the hosts on earth.

verses.translation_literal: For on you I have borne reproach; humiliation has covered my face.
verses.translation_dramatic: It is for you that I have carried this scorn. Shame has covered my face like a cloth.
verses.directors_commentary: 'For on you': the preposition is literal, the speaker has carried the reproach 'upon you', as a man carries a burden for someone else. He has taken the blows meant for God. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read it plainly: they mock him because he serves God, and if he had joined them they would have loved him. The KJV's 'for thy sake' is right in sense, but loses the weight of the carried load that the verb 'nasa'' ('to lift, carry') puts on the speaker's back. 'Shame has covered my face' is a picture to play physically: a hand, a cloak over the face, the head turned from the crowd. In the ancient world the face is where honour sits, and to have it covered is to have lost standing in the community. The Hebrew uses two words for disgrace in the one verse, 'cherpah' and 'klimmah', as the psalm will keep doing.

philological_notes.note: 'I have lifted, carried reproach': the verb gives the scorn weight, as a load. Metzudat David reads the reproach as borne for God's sake.

verses.translation_literal: Estranged I have become to my brothers, and a foreigner to the sons of my mother.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have become a stranger to my own brothers, a foreigner to my mother's sons.
verses.directors_commentary: The cost of loyalty to God is the family. 'Brothers' and 'sons of my mother' say the same thing in two ways, and the second is the sharper, because in a household with several wives, full siblings are a separate and closer bond than half-brothers. To be foreign to your mother's sons is to be cut off from the people closest to you in an ancient clan, where the family is the only safety against the law, the court and hunger. Ibn Ezra and Rashi take the words in other directions: Ibn Ezra, that the speaker has changed so much his brother does not know him; Rashi, with Radak and Metzudat David, hears Esau and Ishmael, the nations. The KJV's 'stranger' and 'alien' are good words, though the second one sounds today like a visitor from space: the Hebrew 'nokhri' is simply a foreigner, someone from another people who does not share your duties. Play it with a lowered voice, because the danger has become domestic.

philological_notes.note: A passive participle of the root 'to be strange': 'one made a stranger'. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'so changed that his brother does not know him'.
A foreigner, a person of another people. It is the opposite of a member of the household.

verses.translation_literal: For the zeal of your house has eaten me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.
verses.translation_dramatic: It is for your house that I burn, and the burning has eaten me away. And every taunt flung at you by your mockers has fallen, like a stone, on me.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the center of the speech, where he says why he suffers, and the actor should let the voice grow quieter, not louder. 'Zeal' (qin'ah) is the same word as jealousy: it is the passion of a man who cannot bear to see what he loves dishonoured. 'House' is the Temple, and the reading splits on who has it. Radak takes it that foreigners now hold sway over the house while he stands outside, and Meiri says he is jealous at seeing it in their hands. Rashi reads it differently: the nations saw the love God showed Israel while the Temple stood, and envied. Metzudat David has the nations envying the glory of the Temple, so that they consume him and add insults to it. The Hebrew allows all of these; a director need only choose one.

The KJV 'eaten me up' keeps the Hebrew verb, which is literally 'ate me', and the image of a passion devouring its host is strong; the BBE's 'on fire with passion' loses the eating. The second line is a chain of the same root, 'reproaches of those who reproach' (cherpot chorfeikha): the mockery aimed at God lands on the one who is loyal to him. Radak says these are the very exiles' enemies who say there will be no return. John 2:17 applies the first line to Jesus in the Temple; that is a later reading, and not the psalm's own setting.

philological_notes.note: 'Zeal' or 'jealousy', the same word. The speaker's passion for God's house is that of one who will not tolerate its dishonour. The envy of others (Rashi, Metzudat David) is a second reading of the same word: the nations are jealous of Israel, and he is jealous for the Temple.

'Your house'. Radak on Psalm 69:10 and Meiri on Psalm 69:10 read it as the Temple, now in foreign hands; Rashi on Psalm 69:10 reads it as the Temple while it still stood, and the divine love that was shown to Israel then. Ibn Ezra on Psalm 69:10 says that the enemies mocked the house where the Ark was kept.

'The reproaches of your reproachers', the noun and participle from one root set side by side. Metzudat Zion on Psalm 69:10 glosses 'fallen' (nafelu) as 'settled, dwelt', as in 'it fell upon the face of all its brothers' in Genesis 25:18, so the taunts have come to lodge on him.

verses.translation_literal: And I wept with the fasting of my soul, and it became reproaches to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I wept, and I fasted, and my very self went hungry for you. And they turned even that into scorn.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker does what a pious person does in trouble: weeps, fasts. The mockers make it a laughing-stock. Rashi and Metzudat David say that they jeer at his prayers, saying that if God had not rejected him He would hear his cries. This is the cruelty of a world where religious acts are public: even the signs of mourning can be used against the mourner. The grammar is knotted. Meiri lists three ways to read 'va'evkeh vatzom nafshi': 'I wept in the fasting of my soul', 'I wept and fasted' with a missing 'and' (Radak), or 'I wept my soul' as if it were dead. The KJV, 'chastened my soul with fasting', is a paraphrase that drops the word for weeping from its place and adds 'chastened'; the Hebrew simply says 'the fasting of my soul', and 'nefesh' is the person himself, not a thing he disciplines. The final phrase, 'it became reproaches to me', is plural, as if each tear or each missed meal drew its own insult.

philological_notes.note: 'In the fasting of my soul': the person himself fasts. Meiri lists the readings: a missing 'and' (Radak), or the soul as the object of weeping.
Plural 'reproaches': each act became a separate insult. Metzudat David says the mockers use his weeping as ground for saying God has not heard him.

verses.translation_literal: And I made my clothing sackcloth, and I became a byword to them.
verses.translation_dramatic: I put on sackcloth for my clothes. And to them I became a byword.
verses.directors_commentary: Sackcloth is the coarse, dark cloth of goat hair, worn next to the skin in mourning and repentance: a public sign that a person has stopped caring how he looks. The speaker 'gives' it as his clothing (the verb 'natan', 'to put, make'), as a deliberate act. And again the world makes a joke of it. 'Mashal' is a byword, a proverb, a saying people use to mean 'as miserable as that one'. Radak says they use his name for anything bad; Meiri and Metzudat David, that it becomes a thing to mock. The KJV's 'a proverb' is correct, and BBE's 'they said evil of me' drops the image. There is a note of the later prophets here: a person who becomes a 'mashal' is a person whose fate others cite as a warning. Play it flat; the psalm has stopped pleading and is simply reporting.

philological_notes.note: Sackcloth, coarse mourning cloth. Meiri takes the wearing of it as a sign of great worry.
A byword, a proverb, a figure of comparison. Radak says they remember him for every bad thing; Meiri reads it as mockery and scorn.

verses.translation_literal: They talk about me, [those] sitting [in] the gate, and [the] songs of drinkers of strong drink.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the gate, where the elders sit and the city's business is done, they talk about me. And in the taverns, over the cups, the drinkers strum their songs, and I am the tune.
verses.directors_commentary:
The city gate was the ancient town hall and law court: elders and judges sat there, deals were sealed and verdicts given. So the first mockers are the respectable ones, the men of standing, and the second group are the lowest: tavern drinkers. Respect and disgrace are both against him, top and bottom of society. Metzudat David notes that it is a shame for judges to waste speech on trifles.

The KJV says 'I was the song of the drunkards', which smooths the Hebrew into a sentence. The Hebrew only says 'and songs of drinkers of strong drink': nothing is said about 'I', and the effect is of music rising from a drinking house with the speaker as its subject. The verb ישיחו (yasichu) is 'muse, chatter, discuss'; here it is gossip that stays on one man.

philological_notes.note: 'Those sitting [at] the gate': the elders and judges who gathered at the city gate to hear cases. The mockers include the city's leaders.
'Stringed songs'. The word names music played on strings, not mere talk, so the mockery is turned into a tune sung in drink.

verses.translation_literal: And I, my prayer [is] to you, YHWH, a time of favor; God, in the greatness of your covenant loyalty, answer me, in [the] faithfulness of your salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I, I have a prayer, and it is for you, LORD. Let this be a time of favor. O God, by the greatness of your faithful love, answer me, answer me by the truth of your rescue.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'and I' (va'ani) is the turn of the psalm: after the gate and the taverns, he has only one audience. Actors should let the pronoun carry a pivot, from what they say to what he says.

'A time of favor' (et ratzon) is a time when God is pleased to receive prayer; the sentence has no verb, so it is a hope or a statement of timing, and commentators split (Rashi: let my prayer's time be a time of favor). The KJV 'acceptable time' is fair. But the KJV renders חֶסֶד as 'mercy', which loses its weight: chesed is covenant loyalty, the bond God has sworn. The prayer rests on that bond, not on the speaker's merit. 'Truth of your salvation' means salvation that proves the promise reliable; Radak: let your promise be proved true.

philological_notes.note: 'A time of favor': the moment when prayer finds acceptance. The phrase has no verb and could be a wish or a statement.
Covenant loyalty, faithful love: a bond-based kindness. 'Mercy' (KJV) is too weak and suggests only pity.

verses.translation_literal: Rescue me from [the] mud, and let me not sink; let me be rescued from those who hate me, and from [the] depths of water.
verses.translation_dramatic: Pull me out of the mud before I sink. Pull me clear of those who hate me, and out of the deep water.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker is in a double picture: the body of water and the crowd of haters, shown side by side without telling which is the image. Radak and Metzudat David read the mud as a picture of troubles; Malbim hears two fears answered by two requests, the mud against the earlier 'I sink', the haters against the deep waters. The 'and' before 'from the depths' can mean 'as if': to be saved from haters is like being saved from the depths of water (Radak).

The mud (tit) is the silt of a pit or of a river bank, where a person can sink and cannot climb out; the audience, in a land of cisterns and wadis, would know the fear. The KJV 'mire' is fine and 'deep waters' is slightly softened from the plural 'depths' (ma'amakkim), which is a word for the deepest places, of the sea or of a flood.

philological_notes.note: 'From mud/silt': the wet clay of a pit bottom or a river bed, in which a person sinks. A picture of troubles.
'Depths of water', a plural of intensity; the Hebrew names the deepest places, not a mere 'deep'.

verses.translation_literal: Let not [the] flood of water overflow me, and let not [the] deep swallow me, and let not [the] pit shut its mouth over me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not let the flood sweep me away. Do not let the deep swallow me. Do not let the pit close its mouth over my head.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three prayers, each opening with the same word 'al' (do not): flood, deep, pit. The three pictures narrow and darken: water that sweeps, water that swallows, a hole that closes. Read it as one voice sinking.

The KJV 'waterflood' is archaic. The Hebrew shibbolet is a flowing stream or a flood and also an ear of grain (the word is the password in Judges 12); here it is the rushing water. The 'pit' (be'er) is usually a well or cistern: a mouth that can be shut on a person like a lid on a hole. Rashi reads it as a foreign trouble that opens its mouth to swallow him; Radak says the pit is the exile. The KJV 'her mouth' follows the feminine 'its', which in English reads oddly as a person. The verb ta'tar is 'shut, close' and Rashi ties it to the left-handed Ehud, 'closed of his right hand' (Judges 3:15).

philological_notes.note: 'Flood, flowing stream', as well as 'ear of grain'. Here a surging current.
'Shut, close': Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion connect it to 'itter yad yemino' (Judges 3:15), a man whose right hand is closed or bound. The pit would close and he cannot climb out.

verses.translation_literal: Answer me, YHWH, for good [is] your covenant loyalty; according to [the] greatness of your compassion, turn to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Answer me, LORD. Your faithful love is good. By all the greatness of your compassion, turn and look at me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker gives a reason with 'for': God should answer because his loyalty is good. He does not argue his own innocence here. Radak: your loyalty is good for me, and though I sin, turn to me by your compassion, not by my deeds.

Here 'rachamim' is 'compassion', from rechem, the womb: the tenderness of a parent. The KJV 'tender mercies' catches that. The same phrase 'greatness of' (rov) appeared in verse 14 for chesed and now returns for rachamim, so the speaker piles up God's own words on God. 'Turn to me' (peneh elai) is a turn of the face, and it sets up the next verse about the hidden face.

philological_notes.note: 'Your compassion': plural of intensity, from the root for the womb, so a parent's love for a child. KJV 'tender mercies' keeps this.

verses.translation_literal: And do not hide your face from your servant, for it is narrow for me; hurry, answer me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not hide your face from your servant. I am in a tight place. Hurry, answer me.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Hiding the face' is the ancient Near Eastern picture of a ruler or god who turns away: no audience, no favor. Radak: one who does not want a man hides his face from him. The speaker calls himself 'your servant' (avdekha), the voice of a subject appealing to his lord and a claim on that lord's care.

The Hebrew 'tzar li' is literally 'it is narrow for me', the same root as 'tzar' (distress, adversary) that is turned toward the narrow place in which the speaker stands, after the image of the pit. The KJV 'I am in trouble' loses the narrowness. The last words, 'maher aneni', are short and clipped: the verse ends in a gasp.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'it is narrow for me': constriction, tight space, hence distress. The same root gives 'tzorerai', my adversaries, in verse 20.

verses.translation_literal: Draw near to my self, redeem it; on account of my enemies, ransom me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Come close to my soul and buy it back. Because of my enemies, set me free.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two legal words of rescue sit side by side. Ga'al is the work of the family redeemer, the go'el, a near kinsman who buys back a relative sold into debt or avenges a death. Padah is to ransom, to pay the price that frees. The pairing makes God the next of kin of the speaker: 'draw near' (qarvah) belongs to the redeemer, because only a close relative could redeem. Malbim: God's closeness to the soul is the ground of redemption.

The KJV 'redeem it: deliver me' does not distinguish the two verbs; 'nefesh', rendered 'soul', is the whole living self, the life and the throat, and ga'alah is also 'redeem it', with the object suffix on the verb. 'Because of my enemies' (lema'an oyevai): Radak says, so that they will not say you have no power to ransom.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of ga'al with 'it' (the nefesh) as object: act as the kinsman-redeemer for it. Ibn Ezra offers other readings, including 'its redemption'.
'Ransom me': pay the price that sets free; the legal partner of ga'al.

verses.translation_literal: You, you know my reproach and my shame and my disgrace; before you [are] all my adversaries.
verses.translation_dramatic: You know it, you. You know my reproach, my shame, my disgrace. And all those who press me are standing before you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker calls out three words for dishonor: cherpah (reproach, taunt), bosheth (shame) and kelimmah (disgrace, the blush of public humiliation). Radak: all kinds of disgrace are listed. In an honor-shame world this was a social death, not a mood. The first word is 'attah', an emphatic 'you': God is the one witness who knows.

The KJV 'thou hast known' puts the past tense where the Hebrew perfect states a present fact, 'you know'; the last clause has no verb: 'before you, all my adversaries', as in a court where the accused stand before the judge. Radak: nothing is hidden from you; they think you do not see them, but you do.

philological_notes.note: A list of three terms for dishonor, with a rising scale: taunt, shame and disgrace, which together give the whole of public humiliation.

verses.translation_literal: Reproach has broken my heart, and I am sick; and I waited for sympathy, and there was none, and for comforters, and I did not find [them].
verses.translation_dramatic: Their scorn has broken my heart, and I am sick with it. I waited for one person to grieve with me, and no one came. I looked for comforters, and found none.
verses.directors_commentary:
The heart (lev) is the center of a person's life, and 'shavrah' says it is broken like a pot. Malbim hears a blow near to death: the word anushah is an incurable wound (Micah 1:9, 2 Samuel 12:15, as Rashi cites). The speaker has been shamed past recovery.

The second half is about comfort that does not come. 'Lanud' is to show sympathy, literally to shake or nod the head in mourning, as Job's friends came 'to console him' (Job 2:11, Rashi). So the speaker waits for a visit of condolence, the ritual people owed the grieving, and no one shows. The KJV 'I looked for some to take pity' is a free paraphrase; the Hebrew 'and I waited' (va'akaveh) is a verb of hope, to wait on a rope drawn taut. The word order puts 'reproach' first, as the cause.

philological_notes.note: 'And I am sick, beyond cure'. A rare form: the alef of the root (as in 'and I loved' in Malachi 1:2) is explained by Rashi and Radak, who read it as 'and I was made sick'. The root names an incurable wound.
'To show sympathy', literally to shake the head or to wander toward a mourner. Rashi ties it to the friends of Job, who came to comfort him.

verses.translation_literal: And they put bitter herb in my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.
verses.translation_dramatic: They put bitterness in my bread. And when I was thirsty, they gave me vinegar to drink.
verses.directors_commentary:
The cruelty is in the feast of comfort turned upside down. 'Baruti' is food, in particular the meal of recovery (2 Samuel 13: 'bring the food' to Tamar's sick brother; Rashi), and Malbim hears the mourner's meal that neighbors bring to the bereaved; here it is laced with bitterness. In the ancient Near East, to share food was to show friendship. Giving bitter food to a hungry man is the opposite of hospitality.

The KJV has 'gall'; the Hebrew 'rosh' is a bitter plant, named with wormwood in Deuteronomy 29:17 (Metzudat Zion). Modern 'poison' (BBE and STEPBible) goes further than the Hebrew. 'Chometz' is soured wine, sharp and cheap, the drink of laborers, here as insult to the thirsty. The verb 'yashkuni' is causative: they made me drink.

philological_notes.note: A bitter plant, named beside wormwood (Deut 29:17); 'gall' in KJV, 'poison' in some modern versions. 'Bitter herb' is the safest sense.
'In my food': a meal, esp. the meal given to the sick or mourning (2 Sam 13:5-6, 10).

verses.translation_literal: May their table before them become a trap, and for [their] well-being, a snare.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let their own table, spread before them, become a trap. And what they trust for their peace, let it turn into a snare.
verses.directors_commentary:
The curse mirrors the crime of the last verse: they set a poisoned table for him, so may their own table turn on them (Ibn Ezra and Radak: this answers 'in my food'). It is the ancient law of the like for like, spoken aloud, and in the Psalms this kind of curse is a request that God bring justice, not a plan for private revenge.

A 'pach' is a bird trap, baited with food (Malbim), and a 'moqesh' a snare that kills. The table, the symbol of hospitality and safety, becomes the bait. The word 'shelomim' is hard. Rashi, Radak and Meiri: 'when they hope for peace (well-being)'; it may also be 'allies', 'peace offerings' or 'recompense' (YLT). The KJV 'that which should have been for their welfare' tracks the first reading. The Hebrew has a pair of nouns with no verb between.

philological_notes.note: 'Their table', the spread cloth or mat on which a meal was set out; the center of hospitality and trust.
Uncertain: 'for [their] well-being' (Rashi, Radak, Meiri), 'for allies' or 'for peace-offerings' (other vocalisations), or 'recompense'. I follow the first.

verses.translation_literal: May their eyes grow dark from seeing, and their loins continually make [them] totter.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let their eyes go dark, so that they cannot see the ground in front of them. And their loins, the seat of a man's strength, let them give way, again and again, until nothing under them holds.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the curse turns for the first time to direct address: until now the speaker has only wished things on his enemies in the third person, but 'hamʿad', 'make [them] shake', is an imperative aimed straight at God. Play it as a man who has run out of patience with wishing and now gives God an order. The two images belong together. Blind eyes mean men cannot see where they step, and weak loins mean legs that cannot hold them. Radak notes that the loins stand for a man's strength and bearing, and he reads the stumbling as a fall from rank and pride; Malbim has them walk blindly into the trap of verse 23 and be caught in it. The KJV 'make their loins continually to shake' is accurate but gives no sense of the Hebrew's physical register, in which the whole lower body fails. The KJV also turns 'from seeing' into the clause 'that they see not', which is fair. Nothing here is a polemic against other gods; it is a judicial blow on the body, the same pairing of blindness and shaking that Deuteronomy 28:28-29 lists among the curses of the covenant.

philological_notes.note: A hiphil imperative: 'make [them] slip, totter'. The root is about feet losing their footing; here it is applied to the loins, which are the centre of strength. Meiri compares Job 13:21 for the same hiphil form; Radak and Metzudat Zion take it as dislodging or sliding.

verses.translation_literal: Pour out upon them your indignation, and the burning of your anger, may it overtake them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Pour it out on them, your fury, as water is poured from a jar until the jar is empty. And let the burning of your anger run them down, and catch them, and hold.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalmist turns here from his own sufferings to the harshest asking in the song, so play it as the voice of a man who has no other court. Pouring is the language of liquid: שָׁפַךְ is the verb for blood and for water, and the picture is a flood from above, not a slow punishment. Then the image changes from liquid to fire and to pursuit: the 'burning' of the anger is a hunter, and יַשִּׂיגֵם, 'may it overtake them', is the word for catching a fleeing man. Note the irony the Hebrew sets up, since the enemies have been the pursuers (v. 27 says 'they pursue'), and now the pursuit is turned around. Ibn Ezra reads the verb as linked to what went before: if they run away, the anger will still catch them. The KJV's 'let thy wrathful anger take hold of them' softens the burning and turns a chase into a grip; the ASV's 'fierceness' is closer to חָרוֹן, from the root 'to burn'. Malbim, working from a different angle, says the indignation is the curse itself and the burning anger is the messenger that carries it.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'the burning of your nose'. The nose, snorting in heat, is the Hebrew picture of anger, and the phrase is a standing formula for God's anger. English 'wrath' or 'anger' loses the heat and the face.
Hiphil of נשג, 'to reach, overtake'. The verb is used for a pursuer catching up; here the anger is the pursuer. Radak says it means that they cannot escape.

verses.translation_literal: May their encampment be desolate; in their tents, may there not be a dweller.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let their camp be left a waste. Let their tents stand open to the wind, and in all of them, not one soul sitting by a fire.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a curse of emptiness: the worst end an ancient household can imagine is not death, it is silence where people used to live. The טִירָה is the walled or stone-built encampment of a settled clan, the thing a family built to last, and the אֹהֶל is the tent, the temporary dwelling. Malbim notices the pairing: the lasting dwelling is to be a desolation, and even the tents, which move from place to place, are to have no one in them. The sense is total: no permanent house, not even a temporary shelter. The KJV's 'habitation' is an archaism that flattens the difference between the two words, and YLT's 'tower' is a more specific guess than the Hebrew supports. Radak and Metzudat Zion gloss the word as 'palace', which comes from Song of Songs 8:9 ('a tower of silver'); that fits a walled compound of wealth. In the Hebrew world, a curse of this kind was heard as a legal sentence, an eviction by God.

philological_notes.note: A walled enclosure, a stone-built encampment or compound. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as 'palace' on the strength of Song 8:9.
A negative jussive, 'let there not be anyone dwelling'. The participle 'dweller' is singular and indefinite, so the emptiness is complete: not one.

verses.translation_literal: For you, [those] whom you struck, they have pursued; and to the pain of your fatally wounded they recount.
verses.translation_dramatic: For it was you who struck him down, and they are the ones who chase the man you have wounded. They sit together and tell it over, the sufferings of those you have left half dead, as if the pain were a story to share.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker's argument is about timing and cruelty. His enemies chase a man God has already struck, which is as dishonourable as kicking someone who is down. Rashi and Meiri point to Zechariah 1:15: God was angry only a little, and they helped for evil, when they should have pitied and helped. Radak makes a different point, that the enemies have power over the speaker only because God has struck him first, so that what they do is part of what God has allowed. Malbim hears them saying openly that the man is God's victim and so fair game. The second half has a hard verb: 'yesapperu' is 'they count' or 'recount', with the preposition 'el', 'to' or 'concerning'. Ibn Ezra and Radak hear them telling one another about their victims' wounds; Meiri hears them plotting in council how to increase the pain. Radak reads 'ḥalalekha' as 'near death', since a corpse feels no pain. The KJV 'talk to the grief' is vague, and the ASV 'tell of the sorrow' is closer; the BBE 'make bitter the grief' goes further than the Hebrew and imposes an action the verb does not name. Play the second line as quiet, gloating talk, not shouting.

philological_notes.note: 'Your pierced, fatally wounded ones'. The word normally means one slain by the sword; Radak and Metzudat David read it as 'near death', because a dead man feels no pain, and the verse speaks of their pain.
A piel of 'to count, recount': they tell it over, as a tale or as a plan. Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as telling one another; Meiri as counselling in their councils.

verses.translation_literal: Put iniquity upon their iniquity, and may they not come into your righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lay guilt upon their guilt, until the weight is more than they can bear; and let them not be let in at the door of your justice.
verses.directors_commentary: The two words for 'iniquity' are the same word, עָוֺן, and the verse leans on that repetition: iniquity on top of iniquity. The sense is not 'make them sin more', as the KJV and ASV 'add iniquity unto their iniquity' can suggest to an English ear. עָוֺן in Hebrew means the crooked deed and also its guilt and its penalty, so the line asks that the account be tallied and paid. YLT and BBE read it as punishment; Radak says it means punishment for their wrongs. Metzudat David reads it as 'count this sin as well, add it to the rest', and Malbim thinks the new sin is their claim that God struck the victim. Meiri compares Genesis 15:16, 'the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full'. Then the second line: צִדְקָה is God's saving justice, the faithful help he gives to his own, and 'come into' it is the language of entering a house or a company. Radak reads it as the good God does for all Israel, or the world to come; Meiri says it means 'mercy', that God should not pity them. To enter God's righteousness is to be on the right side of his judgment, and the plea is that they not be.

philological_notes.note: Iniquity, from a root 'to bend, make crooked'. The word covers the wrong act, the guilt it leaves, and the punishment that follows, so 'put iniquity upon iniquity' can mean a growing debt.
God's righteousness, in the Psalms often his saving justice toward the oppressed. 'Come into it' means to share in it.

verses.translation_literal: May they be wiped out from the scroll of life, and with the righteous may they not be written.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let their names be rubbed from the scroll of the living, and never be inked in beside the righteous.
verses.directors_commentary: The scene is a register, a roll of names. Ancient communities kept lists of their citizens, and to be struck off the list was to lose one's place and one's share, and here the list is God's. The verb מָחָה, 'wipe out', is the word for wiping a writing surface clean, and the second line makes the writing explicit: 'may they not be written'. The two lines say the same thing in two ways, and Radak says so. The KJV 'book of the living' keeps the Hebrew חַיִּים, plural 'life', closer than the ASV 'book of life'. Whether the book is this life or the next is disputed in the notes in the packet: Ibn Ezra says the book is heaven, where all decrees are written at creation; Radak and Meiri read it as the life of the world to come; Metzudat David says that if they were already written, they should be erased, and if not, they should not be added. The Hebrew does not choose, and an actor should not either. The image of a divine register has a close cousin in Exodus 32:32, where Moses asks to be blotted out of the book God has written.

philological_notes.note: 'The scroll of life', or 'of the living'. A roll of those who are to live. Ibn Ezra says the heavens are the book; Radak and Meiri say it is the life of the world to come.
Niphal jussive of מחה, 'to wipe, to blot out'; the verb for erasing writing, also used of wiping a dish clean (2 Kings 21:13).

verses.translation_literal: And I, afflicted and in pain, your salvation, O God, may it set me on high.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I am bowed and aching. Let your rescue, O God, lift me up out of reach.
verses.directors_commentary: The whole turn of the psalm sits on the first word, 'and I', set against 'they' in the verses before. Everything before was about what the enemies do; now one voice stands apart: 'And I'. The two words, עָנִי and כוֹאֵב, 'afflicted' and 'in pain', answer the enemies' telling of other men's pain in v. 27, since the same root כאב is used there, so he claims for himself the pain they gossip about. The wordplay in the second half is on height: תְּשַׂגְּבֵנִי, 'set me on high', is from שָׂגַב, to be out of reach, the word for a fortress on a rock. The picture is the opposite of being pursued and caught (v. 25): the man who was run down is lifted beyond the reach of the hunters. The KJV 'poor' for עָנִי is not wrong, but the word means someone bowed down and made low by others, which is the sense that sets up the contrast with height. Ibn Ezra reads the verse as a pair, 'afflicted' with 'on high'. Malbim says it contradicts the enemies' claim that God struck him.

philological_notes.note: 'Afflicted, bowed down', from a root meaning to be made low or oppressed. In the Psalms it is the typical word for the weak who depend on God.
Piel of שגב, 'to be high, inaccessible'; the noun מִשְׂגָּב is a stronghold or refuge. The word means to set someone out of the enemy's reach.

token_glosses.gloss: may it set me on high

verses.translation_literal: I will praise the name of God with a song, and I will magnify him with thanksgiving.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will praise the name of God in a song, and make him great with thanks.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood changes completely: the curses stop and a vow begins, in the first person cohortative that is a promise to do something once help has come. 'Praise' and 'magnify' are the two verbs of a thank-offering. הִלֵּל is the root of 'hallelujah', and גִּדֵּל is 'to make great', so the speaker promises to enlarge God in the eyes of others by speaking of him, since God does not literally grow. The word בְּתוֹדָה is the key to the next verse: תּוֹדָה is both 'thanks' and the name of the thanksgiving sacrifice, the offering with a communal meal that a rescued person brings to the sanctuary (Lev 7:12). Radak says it means exactly that: he will give thanks for God's kindness and bring a thanksgiving offering. The KJV's 'with thanksgiving' hides that double sense of word and offering. The same sense of singing and sacrifice together explains why the next verse sets song against animal.

philological_notes.note: 'Thanks, confession', and the name of the thanksgiving sacrifice. Radak reads it as the offering that goes with the praise.
Piel of גדל, 'to make great'. Praise enlarges God's name in the hearing of others.

verses.translation_literal: And it will be good to YHWH, [more] than an ox, a young bull, horned, hooved.
verses.translation_dramatic: And that will please the LORD more than any sacrifice of ox or bullock, the fullgrown beast with its horns and its split hooves, the best a man could bring.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker has just promised song and thanksgiving, and now he claims that this will please God more than a sacrifice. Audiences hear a shock here: the most costly offering a farmer could bring is ranked below a poem. The Hebrew has no conjunction between 'shor' and 'par', but that does not mean one animal. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri read the mem of 'mishor' as serving both words, 'than an ox, than a bull', and so understand two animals, the ox as the larger and the bull as the smaller. The KJV 'ox or bullock' therefore follows them and is a fair rendering. Metzudat Zion instead reads one phrase with two synonyms for extra clarity, so 'ox, bull'. The last two words describe the animal: 'maqrin' has horns, 'mafris' has divided hooves, which makes it mature and, by Leviticus 11:3, clean. Radak and Meiri add that a young animal's hooves are soft before its horns grow, so the phrase names a fully grown beast; Radak adds that this is the age fit for sacrifice. Rashi and the Targum tell a story that this was Adam's ox, made with horns before hooves; that is midrash, and the Hebrew does not say it.

philological_notes.note: Hebrew has no 'or' here. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri read the mem as serving both nouns, hence two animals, an ox and a bull; Metzudat Zion reads one phrase of synonyms, which stresses the size of the offering.

Two hiphil participles, 'making horns' and 'splitting the hoof': an animal with horns and cloven hooves. Radak and Meiri read it as marking a fully grown beast, since the hooves of a young one are soft.

verses.translation_literal: They have seen, the humble; they rejoice. You who seek God, and may your heart live.
verses.translation_dramatic: The humble have seen it, and they are glad. You who seek God: let your heart live again.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm now opens its circle: the private voice of one sufferer becomes an address to a crowd. The humble, עֲנָוִים, are a cousin of the 'afflicted' of v. 30, and they are the ones who will watch the rescue and rejoice. The grammar jumps from 'they' to 'you', from third person to second, in the middle of the verse, and Radak and Meiri say this is the habit of prophetic speech, which turns from describing to addressing. The KJV smooths the jump by making everything future. The Hebrew perfect, 'they have seen', is closer to YLT: Meiri says a past form stands for the future, as the voice of someone who sees it already done. The last line is a striking idiom: וִיחִי לְבַבְכֶם, 'may your heart live'. In the ancient world a heart sunk in worry is called dead, and Radak, Metzudat David and others say exactly this: a man who is anxious and in pain is as dead, and joy brings the heart to life. So 'live' here is the opposite of the 'scroll of life' fear: the hearers' hearts are to come back from the dead.

philological_notes.note: 'May your heart live', meaning revive. Radak and Metzudat David say a heart weighed down by worry counts as dead, and joy gives it life.
'The humble, the meek', those who bear affliction without bitterness. Malbim says they accept in love whatever comes to them.

verses.translation_literal: For YHWH is listening to the needy, and his prisoners he has not despised.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD bends his ear to the poor, and those of his own who sit in chains, he has not scorned.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the reason for the joy of the last verse, and it is the quiet center of the psalm: God listens. The verb שֹׁמֵעַ followed by אֶל means to listen toward someone, to turn the ear, and it is a participle, so it is a continuing fact, not a single event. The pairing is 'the needy' אֶבְיוֹנִים and 'his prisoners' אֲסִירָיו. The KJV 'the poor' covers the first but the second word is stronger than it seems: אָסִיר is a man in chains, a prisoner, and the possessive 'his' means they are bound but still God's own. Radak says they are the people in exile, bound but still his, and that the nations will say, when they are freed, that God heard them. Metzudat David says they were bound because they rebelled against God, and even so he has not despised their prayer. The KJV's 'despiseth not' is right; the verb בָּזָה is to treat as worthless. Malbim says the suffering of the righteous was never a sign that God did not see them, and this answers the lament of the first half of the psalm, where the speaker feared he was forgotten.

philological_notes.note: 'His prisoners', those bound. Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as the exiles; Metzudat David says they were bound for rebelling and God still heard their prayer.
'To despise, to hold in contempt'. The perfect here describes a settled attitude: he has never done it and does not.

verses.translation_literal: Let them praise him, heaven and earth, the seas, and every creeping thing in them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let heaven and earth praise him, and the seas, and everything that stirs and crawls within them.
verses.directors_commentary: From the humble of one city the song widens to the whole world: sky, land and sea, and everything that moves. The Hebrew order is the same three-part world as in Genesis 1, heaven, earth, seas, and the last word רֹמֵשׂ is a Genesis word too: the 'creeping thing' that God made on the sixth day. The KJV 'every thing that moveth' is too general, and loses the picture of low, crawling creatures, the smallest beasts joining a chorus. Ibn Ezra offers two readings: either the beings who live in these places, or a poetic figure like 'the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing'. Radak and Meiri read it as a figure, that joy will spread through the whole world. Metzudat David says the host of heaven and the dwellers of earth and sea will praise him on account of the rescue. The pronoun בָּם, 'in them', is plural and covers all three realms. Call it a cosmic hallelujah: a psalm that opens with water up to the neck ends with the seas themselves singing.

philological_notes.note: 'Creeping thing, that which moves low along the ground', the word used in Genesis 1:24-26 for crawling creatures. Metzudat Zion links it to the verb for treading.
Piel jussive of הלל, 'let them praise him'. The same root as the singer's own vow in v. 31, so heaven and earth take up the singer's song.

verses.translation_literal: For God, he will save Zion, and he will build the cities of Judah, and they will dwell there, and they will possess it.
verses.translation_dramatic: For God himself will save Zion. He will raise up the cities of Judah stone by stone, and his people will come home and live there, and the land will be theirs again.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns on its last word-pair: after thirty-five verses of drowning, mud and thirst, the singer stops speaking of himself and speaks of the city. Play it as a lifted head, not a shout. The verb for "save" (yoshia') is the same root as the cry that opens the psalm, "Save me, O God" (hoshiʿeni, 69:2), so the personal plea becomes a national promise: the one who is asked to save the singer will save Zion.

The KJV's "that they may dwell there" turns the Hebrew into a purpose clause. The Hebrew has no "that": it is a plain chain of futures, "and he will build... and they will dwell... and they will possess it", each step following the last. Note too the sequence: God builds first, and only then do people settle. Mentioning the "cities of Judah" beside Zion makes this a statement about a ruined or emptied country, which is why many readers hear the exile behind it. Meiri takes "Judah" as a name for all the exiles under the rule of David's house; Radak says Zion and Judah are named as the core, and the rest of Israel is included. There is also a quiet reversal of the singer's own curse in 69:26, "Let their encampment be desolate; in their tents let there be no dweller (אַל־יְהִי יֹשֵׁב)": the enemies' tents are emptied of dwellers, while Judah's cities fill with them (veyashevu, "and they will dwell"). The verb "dwell" returns in the next verse as well.

The final verb, "possess it" (vireshuha), is the language of the land-grant: yarash is the word for taking a territory by right. It carries the old conquest vocabulary, applied now to a return. Note the feminine "it": the object is Zion (a feminine noun), or the land as a whole, as Radak says.

philological_notes.note: "He will save", imperfect of the root that gives the psalm its opening cry hoshiʿeni (69:2). The psalm begins and ends with the same verb, moving from one person's rescue to the rescue of a city.

"And they will possess it", with a feminine suffix pointing back to Zion or the land. Radak notes the form is from yarash, with tsere under the resh, comparing it to a verb of inheriting, and says the suffix refers to Zion or the whole land of Israel.

verses.translation_literal: And the seed of his servants, they will inherit it, and the lovers of his name, they will dwell in it.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the children of his servants will hold it as their own, and all who love his name will make their home within it, and rest there.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last line of the psalm, thirty-six verses after the singer first went under the water, is a quiet one. Do not close on triumph; close on settledness. The singer, who began with "the waters have come up to my neck" (69:2) and "let not the flood of water sweep over me" (69:16), ends with people who live somewhere and are not moving. After the cursing, the psalm ends with a house.

Two groups appear: the "seed of his servants" and the "lovers of his name". The first is about family and descent, the land passing from father to child; Metzudat David reads "his servants" as the patriarchs, through whose merit their descendants inherit the land, and Ibn Ezra hears the time of David or of the messiah. The second is about loyalty to God himself: "his name" stands for God's presence, the thing Zion is built to hold. Malbim adds that the inheritance passes to the children without anyone being driven out again, since the lovers of the name will dwell there in peace and quiet. The KJV's "the seed also of his servants" adds "also", which the Hebrew does not have, and "therein" is archaic for "in it"; the BBE's "have their part in it" and "have rest" blur two different verbs, nachal (take as a hereditary holding) and shakan (settle, tabernacle).

The verb shakan is the root of the later word Shekhinah, and of "tabernacle"; it is used for God's dwelling among his people, so an audience might hear "they will dwell" as "they will be where he dwells". The "it" in both verbs is feminine, resuming Zion and the land from the previous verse.

philological_notes.note: "They will inherit it": nachal means to hold land as a family holding passed on by descent, not simply to arrive at it. Metzudat David reads the inheritance as earned through the merit of the fathers.
"They will dwell", a settling verb that is also used for God's presence among his people, so the line is also about living near his name. Malbim hears in it a peaceful, undisturbed dwelling.
